Atrial Fibrillation (AFib).education:
What is Atrial Fibrillation (AFib)?
Atrial fibrillation is a common heart rhythm disorder in which the upper chambers of the heart (atria) beat irregularly and often too fast. This irregular rhythm can reduce the heart's ability to pump blood effectively and may increase the risk of blood clots, stroke, heart failure, and other cardiovascular complications.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Rapid or irregular heartbeat (palpitations)
-Fluttering or pounding sensation in the chest
-Dizziness or lightheadedness
-Fatigue or weakness
-Shortness of breath, especially with activity
-Chest pain or discomfort
-Reduced ability to exercise
-Confusion
-Some people may have no noticeable symptoms

Risk Factors:
-Older age
-High blood pressure
-Heart valve disease
-Coronary artery disease or prior heart attack
-Heart failure
-Obesity
-Diabetes
-Hyperthyroidism
-Sleep apnea
-Chronic lung disease
-Excessive alcohol or caffeine intake
-Family history of AFib
-Prior heart surgery

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications exactly as directed, including blood thinners (anticoagulants), rate-control, or rhythm-control medications.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
-Monitor pulse regularly as directed by the healthcare provider.
-Keep all scheduled cardiology and PCP appointments.
-Limit or avoid alcohol and caffeine as recommended.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Stay physically active as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
-Manage stress through relaxation techniques, exercise, or counseling.
-Report new or worsening palpitations, dizziness, fainting, shortness of breath, or chest pain to the healthcare provider promptly.

Congestive Heart Failure.education:
What is Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)?
Congestive heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart does not pump blood as effectively as it should. This can cause blood and fluid to back up in the lungs, abdomen, and lower extremities. CHF can result from conditions that damage or overwork the heart, such as coronary artery disease, high blood pressure, or heart valve disease.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Shortness of breath, especially with activity or when lying flat
-Persistent coughing or wheezing, sometimes producing white or pink-tinged mucus
-Swelling (edema) of the feet, ankles, legs, or abdomen
-Fatigue or weakness
-Rapid or irregular heartbeat
-Reduced ability to exercise
-Increased need to urinate at night
-Sudden weight gain from fluid retention
-Difficulty concentrating or decreased alertness
-Nausea or loss of appetite

Risk Factors:
-Coronary artery disease or prior heart attack
-High blood pressure
-Diabetes
-Obesity
-Heart valve disease
-Cardiomyopathy or family history of cardiomyopathy
-History of myocarditis
-Congenital heart defects
-Chronic lung disease
-Sleep apnea
-Excessive alcohol use
-Tobacco use
-Older age

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications exactly as directed, including ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, diuretics, or other heart failure medications.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
-Weigh yourself daily at the same time, wearing similar clothing, and record the weight.
-Report weight gain of more than 2-3 pounds in one day or 5 pounds in one week to the healthcare provider.
-Limit sodium intake as directed by the healthcare provider.
-Limit fluid intake if directed by the healthcare provider.
-Stay physically active as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
-Elevate legs when sitting to reduce swelling.
-Get adequate rest and avoid overexertion.
-Keep all scheduled cardiology and PCP appointments.
-Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza and pneumococcal vaccines.
-Avoid tobacco and limit alcohol as directed.

Coronary Artery Disease.education:
What is Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)?
Coronary artery disease is a condition in which the arteries that supply blood and oxygen to the heart become narrowed or blocked due to the buildup of cholesterol and fatty deposits called plaque. Over time, this reduces blood flow to the heart and can increase the risk of chest pain (angina), heart attack, heart failure, and stroke.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Chest pain or pressure (angina), especially with activity or stress
-Shortness of breath
-Fatigue or weakness
-Dizziness or lightheadedness
-Palpitations or irregular heartbeat
-Nausea
-Pain radiating to the arm, shoulder, neck, jaw, or back
-Some people may have no symptoms until a heart attack occurs

Risk Factors:
-High blood pressure
-High cholesterol (dyslipidemia)
-Diabetes
-Smoking or tobacco use
-Overweight or obesity
-Physical inactivity
-Unhealthy diet high in saturated fat, trans fat, cholesterol, and sodium
-Family history of heart disease
-Older age
-Chronic stress
-Excessive alcohol consumption

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications exactly as directed, including cholesterol-lowering, blood pressure, antiplatelet, and other cardiac medications.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
-Follow a heart-healthy diet low in saturated fat, cholesterol, and sodium.
-Engage in regular physical activity as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Stop smoking and avoid secondhand smoke.
-Manage stress through healthy coping strategies.
-Monitor blood pressure and cholesterol levels as recommended.
-Keep all scheduled cardiology and PCP appointments.
-Report chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, fainting, or swelling to the healthcare provider promptly.

Dyslipidemia.education:
What is Dyslipidemia?
Dyslipidemia means having unhealthy levels of cholesterol and/or other fats (lipids) in the blood. High LDL ("bad") cholesterol can contribute to plaque buildup inside the arteries. Over time, plaque buildup can narrow or block blood vessels and increase the risk of heart attack and stroke. Dyslipidemia usually does not cause noticeable symptoms, making routine blood tests important for early detection and management.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Dyslipidemia often has no noticeable symptoms
-Very high cholesterol levels may sometimes cause yellowish deposits under the skin (xanthomas)
-Whitish ring around the cornea of the eye (arcus cornealis)
-Symptoms may not appear until a cardiovascular event such as heart attack or stroke occurs
-Routine blood tests (lipid panel) are the primary way to detect dyslipidemia

Risk Factors:
-Family history of high cholesterol or heart disease
-Diet high in saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol
-Overweight or obesity
-Physical inactivity
-Diabetes
-Hypothyroidism
-Kidney disease
-Liver disease
-Smoking
-Excessive alcohol intake
-Older age
-Certain medications

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take cholesterol-lowering medications (statins or others) exactly as prescribed.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
-Follow a heart-healthy diet low in saturated fat, trans fat, and cholesterol.
-Engage in regular physical activity as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Stop smoking and avoid secondhand smoke.
-Limit alcohol intake as recommended.
-Complete cholesterol and lipid panel testing as ordered by the healthcare provider.
-Keep all scheduled PCP and cardiology appointments.
-Report muscle pain, weakness, or dark-colored urine while taking statin medications to the healthcare provider.

Hypertension.education:
What is Hypertension?
Hypertension (high blood pressure) occurs when the pressure of blood against the walls of the blood vessels stays too high. High blood pressure often has no symptoms. If not controlled, hypertension can increase the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease, vision loss, and other health problems. Controlling blood pressure through medications and healthy lifestyle habits can help reduce these risks.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Hypertension often has no noticeable symptoms
-Very high blood pressure may sometimes be associated with:
  -Severe headache
  -Dizziness
  -Vision changes or blurred vision
  -Chest pain
  -Shortness of breath
  -Nosebleeds
  -Blood in the urine
-Regular blood pressure checks are important even when feeling well

Risk Factors:
-Family history of high blood pressure or heart disease
-Older age
-Being overweight or obese
-Lack of regular physical activity
-Diet high in sodium (salt)
-Excessive alcohol intake
-Tobacco use or exposure to secondhand smoke
-Chronic stress
-Poor sleep or sleep apnea
-Diabetes
-Kidney disease
-Certain medications

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take blood pressure medications exactly as prescribed.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
-Check and record blood pressure at home as directed.
-Sit quietly for at least 5 minutes before taking a reading.
-Keep feet flat on the floor and support the arm at heart level during measurement.
-Bring blood pressure readings to healthcare appointments.
-Notify the healthcare provider if readings are repeatedly outside the recommended range.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Avoid tobacco products and secondhand smoke.
-Limit alcohol as recommended.
-Participate in regular physical activity as tolerated and approved by the healthcare provider.
-Manage stress through relaxation techniques, exercise, hobbies, or counseling.
-Keep all scheduled PCP and cardiology appointments.

Sick Sinus Syndrome.education:
What is Sick Sinus Syndrome (SSS)?
Sick sinus syndrome is a condition in which the heart's natural pacemaker (sinus node) does not work properly. It may cause the heart to beat too slowly, too fast, or irregularly. A pacemaker may be implanted to help maintain an appropriate heart rate.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Dizziness or lightheadedness
-Fainting or near-fainting (syncope)
-Fatigue or weakness
-Shortness of breath
-Palpitations or feeling the heart racing or fluttering
-Chest discomfort
-Confusion or difficulty concentrating
-Pauses in heartbeat
-Some people may have no symptoms

Risk Factors:
-Older age
-History of heart disease or prior heart surgery
-High blood pressure
-Heart valve disease
-Cardiomyopathy
-Myocarditis (inflammation of the heart)
-Medications that slow heart rate
-Congenital heart defects
-Infiltrative diseases affecting the heart

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Keep all scheduled cardiology and pacemaker/device-check appointments.
-Carry the pacemaker identification card and consider wearing medical identification if a pacemaker is implanted.
-Inform healthcare providers, dentists, and other medical professionals about the pacemaker.
-Follow the cardiologist's recommendations regarding physical activity and exercise.
-Check the pacemaker incision/site as directed and report redness, swelling, warmth, drainage, worsening pain, or fever.
-Do not place strong magnets directly over the pacemaker.
-Follow the pacemaker manufacturer's and cardiologist's instructions regarding cell phones, headphones, security systems, and other electronic devices.
-Discuss MRI scans or procedures involving electrical equipment with the healthcare provider before they are performed.
-Take all prescribed medications as directed.
-Report dizziness, fainting, unusual weakness, worsening shortness of breath, or new palpitations to the healthcare provider.

Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm.education:
What is an Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA)?
An abdominal aortic aneurysm is an enlargement or bulge in the aorta, the main blood vessel that carries blood from the heart through the abdomen to the rest of the body. If the aneurysm grows large enough, it can rupture, which is a life-threatening emergency. Most small aneurysms grow slowly and may be monitored; larger aneurysms may require surgical repair.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Most small AAAs cause no symptoms and are found incidentally during imaging
-Deep, constant pain in the abdomen or side of the abdomen
-Back pain
-Pulsating feeling near the navel
-A ruptured AAA causes sudden, severe abdominal or back pain, dizziness, rapid heartbeat, and loss of consciousness

Risk Factors:
-Smoking (strongest risk factor)
-Male sex
-Age 65 or older
-Family history of aortic aneurysm
-High blood pressure
-Atherosclerosis (hardening of the arteries)
-History of other aneurysms
-Connective tissue disorders

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Attend all scheduled follow-up imaging and appointments to monitor aneurysm size.
-Take blood pressure and cholesterol medications as prescribed.
-Stop smoking and avoid all tobacco products.
-Maintain blood pressure within the provider-recommended range.
-Engage in moderate physical activity as approved by the healthcare provider.
-Avoid heavy lifting or straining as directed.
-Report new or worsening abdominal or back pain immediately.
-Notify the healthcare provider of any new pulsating sensation in the abdomen.

PAD.education:
What is Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD)?
Peripheral arterial disease is a circulatory condition in which narrowed or blocked arteries reduce blood flow to the limbs, most commonly the legs. PAD is usually caused by atherosclerosis (plaque buildup in the arteries). It can increase the risk of heart attack, stroke, and critical limb ischemia if left untreated.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Leg pain or cramping during walking or exercise that improves with rest (claudication)
-Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the legs
-Coldness in the lower leg or foot compared to the other side
-Sores or wounds on the toes, feet, or legs that heal slowly or do not heal
-Color changes in the skin of the legs or feet
-Shiny skin on the legs
-Decreased or absent pulse in the feet
-Erectile dysfunction in men
-Some people may have no symptoms

Risk Factors:
-Smoking (strongest risk factor)
-Diabetes
-High blood pressure
-High cholesterol
-Older age (especially over 50)
-Family history of PAD, heart disease, or stroke
-Obesity
-Physical inactivity
-Kidney disease

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications as directed, including antiplatelet, cholesterol, and blood pressure medications.
-Stop smoking and avoid all tobacco products.

PVD.education:
What is Peripheral Vascular Disease (PVD)?
Peripheral vascular disease is a broad term for diseases of the blood vessels outside the heart and brain, most commonly affecting arteries and veins in the legs. PVD includes conditions caused by atherosclerosis (plaque buildup) as well as conditions affecting the veins. PVD can reduce blood flow to the limbs and increase the risk of complications if untreated.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Pain, aching, or cramping in the legs during walking or activity
-Numbness, tingling, or weakness in the legs or feet
-Coldness in the lower legs or feet
-Color changes in the skin (pale, bluish, or reddish)
-Slow-healing sores or wounds on the legs or feet
-Swelling of the legs or ankles (venous disease)
-Varicose veins or skin changes from chronic venous insufficiency
-Reduced hair growth on the legs
-Weak or absent pulses in the legs or feet

Risk Factors:
-Smoking
-Diabetes
-High blood pressure
-High cholesterol
-Older age
-Obesity
-Physical inactivity
-Family history of vascular disease
-History of blood clots

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications as directed.
-Stop smoking and avoid tobacco products.
-Walk and exercise regularly as approved by the healthcare provider.
-Inspect feet and legs daily for cuts, sores, or changes.
-Keep feet clean, dry, and moisturized.
-Wear compression stockings if prescribed for venous disease.
-Elevate legs when sitting to reduce swelling if directed.
-Manage blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol as directed.
-Avoid prolonged sitting or standing without movement.
-Keep all scheduled appointments with the vascular specialist and PCP.
-Report worsening pain, swelling, skin changes, or non-healing wounds.

Asthma.education:
What is Asthma?
Asthma is a chronic condition that causes inflammation and narrowing of the airways. Symptoms can come and go and may range from mild to severe. Asthma can usually be controlled with medications, avoiding triggers, and regular healthcare follow-up.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Shortness of breath
-Wheezing
-Coughing, especially at night or early in the morning
-Chest tightness
-Difficulty breathing
-Symptoms that worsen with exercise, illness, allergies, smoke, or other triggers

Risk Factors:
-Family history of asthma or allergies
-Personal history of allergies (allergic rhinitis, eczema)
-Respiratory infections in childhood
-Exposure to secondhand smoke
-Exposure to air pollution, dust, mold, or chemical fumes
-Obesity
-Occupational exposure to irritants

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take asthma medications exactly as prescribed.
-Use daily controller medication consistently if prescribed.
-Keep the prescribed quick-relief/rescue inhaler readily available at all times.
-Know the difference between controller and rescue medications.
-Use the correct inhaler technique and spacer if prescribed.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
-Notify the healthcare provider if the rescue inhaler is needed more frequently than usual.
-Identify and avoid known asthma triggers.
-Follow the individualized asthma action plan provided by the healthcare provider.
-Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza and COVID-19.
-Keep all scheduled PCP and pulmonology appointments.

COPD.education:
What is Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)?
COPD is a long-term lung disease that causes airflow blockage, making it difficult to breathe. It is most commonly caused by smoking or long-term exposure to lung irritants. Although COPD cannot be cured, it can be managed by taking prescribed medications, using inhalers correctly, avoiding smoking, staying physically active as tolerated, receiving recommended vaccinations, and seeking prompt treatment for worsening symptoms or respiratory infections.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Shortness of breath, especially with activity
-Chronic cough
-Increased mucus (phlegm) production
-Wheezing
-Chest tightness
-Fatigue
-Frequent respiratory infections
-Difficulty taking deep breaths
-Bluish lips or fingernails (cyanosis) in severe cases
-Swelling of the ankles, feet, or legs in advanced disease

Risk Factors:
-Smoking or history of smoking
-Exposure to secondhand smoke
-Long-term exposure to air pollution
-Occupational exposure to dust, fumes, or chemicals
-Older age
-History of asthma
-Family history of COPD or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
-Frequent respiratory infections
-Poor air quality or biomass fuel exposure

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Stop smoking and avoid exposure to lung irritants.
-Take prescribed inhalers and medications as directed.
-Use supplemental oxygen if prescribed.
-Participate in pulmonary rehabilitation if recommended.
-Stay physically active as tolerated.
-Practice breathing techniques, such as pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing.
-Receive recommended vaccinations, including influenza, COVID-19, and pneumococcal vaccines.
-Maintain good nutrition and adequate hydration.
-Seek prompt treatment for respiratory infections.
-Attend regular follow-up appointments with the PCP and pulmonologist.

Cystic Fibrosis.education:
What is Cystic Fibrosis (CF)?
Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disorder that causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs, digestive tract, and other organs. The mucus clogs the airways and traps bacteria, leading to repeated lung infections, progressive lung damage, and difficulty breathing. CF also affects the pancreas, impairing digestion and nutrient absorption.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Persistent cough that produces thick mucus
-Frequent lung infections such as pneumonia and bronchitis
-Wheezing or shortness of breath
-Poor growth or weight gain despite good appetite
-Very salty-tasting skin
-Frequent, greasy, or bulky stools
-Difficulty with bowel movements or intestinal blockage
-Nasal polyps or chronic sinus infections
-Clubbing of the fingers and toes
-Male infertility

Risk Factors:
-Family history of cystic fibrosis (inherited genetic condition)
-Both parents must carry the CF gene mutation
-Most commonly affects Caucasian individuals

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications as directed, including CFTR modulators, mucus-thinning medications, bronchodilators, and antibiotics.
-Perform airway clearance techniques daily as directed.
-Take pancreatic enzyme replacements with meals and snacks as prescribed.
-Take prescribed vitamins and nutritional supplements.
-Maintain a high-calorie, high-fat diet as recommended.
-Stay physically active as tolerated.
-Avoid exposure to cigarette smoke, air pollution, and people who are sick.
-Maintain good hand hygiene.
-Keep all scheduled pulmonology, gastroenterology, and CF clinic appointments.
-Receive recommended vaccinations.

OSA.education:
What is Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)?
OSA is a condition in which the airway becomes blocked or narrowed during sleep, causing breathing to repeatedly stop and start. OSA can lower oxygen levels and interfere with getting restful sleep. Treatment helps improve sleep quality and may reduce the risk of other health problems such as high blood pressure, heart disease, and stroke.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Loud snoring
-Gasping or choking during sleep
-Pauses in breathing while sleeping (witnessed by a bed partner)
-Waking with a dry mouth or sore throat
-Morning headaches
-Feeling tired or sleepy during the daytime
-Difficulty concentrating or memory problems
-Irritability or mood changes
-Frequent nighttime urination

Risk Factors:
-Overweight or obesity
-Large neck circumference
-Narrowed airway
-Male sex
-Older age
-Family history of sleep apnea
-Smoking
-Nasal congestion
-Use of alcohol or sedatives
-Medical conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart failure

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Use CPAP/BiPAP every time you sleep, including naps, as prescribed.
-Do not change the pressure settings unless instructed by the healthcare provider.
-Make sure the mask fits comfortably and securely.
-Clean the mask, tubing, humidifier, and other equipment according to the manufacturer's/provider's instructions.
-Replace filters, masks, tubing, and other supplies as recommended.
-Contact the healthcare provider or equipment supplier for persistent mask leaks, skin irritation, dryness, or difficulty using the device.
-Maintain a healthy weight if recommended.
-Avoid alcohol or sedating medications near bedtime unless approved by the healthcare provider.
-Sleep on your side if recommended by the sleep specialist.
-Keep regular appointments with the sleep specialist.
-Report continued excessive daytime sleepiness or morning headaches despite regular use.

Pulmonary Fibrosis.education:
What is Pulmonary Fibrosis?
Pulmonary fibrosis is a lung disease that occurs when lung tissue becomes scarred and thickened. This scarring makes it difficult for the lungs to function properly and progressively reduces the ability to breathe. The cause is often unknown (idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis), but it can also result from environmental exposures, medications, radiation therapy, or autoimmune conditions.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Shortness of breath, especially with activity
-Dry, persistent cough
-Fatigue and weakness
-Unexplained weight loss
-Aching muscles and joints
-Clubbing (widening and rounding) of the fingertips and toes
-Fast, shallow breathing
-Crackling sounds heard through a stethoscope

Risk Factors:
-Smoking or history of smoking
-Environmental or occupational exposure to dust, asbestos, silica, or other irritants
-Certain medications (chemotherapy, cardiac medications)
-Radiation therapy to the chest
-Autoimmune or connective tissue diseases
-Family history of pulmonary fibrosis
-Older age (usually diagnosed between 50-70)
-Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed antifibrotic medications (pirfenidone or nintedanib) as directed.
-Use supplemental oxygen if prescribed.
-Participate in pulmonary rehabilitation if recommended.
-Stay physically active as tolerated.
-Practice breathing techniques to improve oxygen exchange.
-Receive recommended vaccinations.
-Avoid smoking and exposure to lung irritants.
-Maintain good nutrition.
-Keep all scheduled pulmonology appointments.
-Report worsening shortness of breath, cough, or decreased activity tolerance.
-Discuss lung transplant evaluation with the provider if appropriate.

Diabetes.education:
What is Diabetes?
Diabetes is a condition in which the blood sugar (glucose) level is too high. The body either does not make enough insulin or does not use insulin properly. Over time, uncontrolled diabetes can affect the heart, kidneys, eyes, nerves, and blood vessels. Keeping blood sugar controlled can help prevent or delay complications.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Increased thirst
-Frequent urination
-Increased hunger
-Feeling tired or weak
-Blurred vision
-Unexplained weight loss
-Cuts or wounds that heal slowly
-Frequent infections
-Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
-Some people may have no noticeable symptoms

Risk Factors:
-Family history of diabetes
-Being overweight or obese
-Physical inactivity
-Age 35 or older
-History of prediabetes or gestational diabetes
-High blood pressure or abnormal cholesterol levels
-Certain racial or ethnic groups have an increased risk

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take diabetes medications or insulin exactly as prescribed.
-Check and record blood sugar as directed by the healthcare provider.
-Follow a healthy, balanced meal plan and control carbohydrate portions.
-Limit sugary drinks, sweets, and highly processed foods.
-Eat more vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and high-fiber foods.
-Stay physically active as tolerated and recommended.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Attend routine medical appointments and complete A1C and other recommended laboratory tests.
-Check feet daily for cuts, sores, redness, swelling, or infection.
-Complete routine eye, kidney, and foot examinations as recommended.
-Do not stop or change diabetes medications without consulting the healthcare provider.

Signs of Low Blood Sugar (Hypoglycemia):
-Shaking or sweating
-Hunger
-Dizziness or weakness
-Fast heartbeat
-Headache
-Irritability or confusion

Signs of High Blood Sugar (Hyperglycemia):
-Increased thirst
-Frequent urination
-Blurred vision
-Fatigue or weakness
-Headache
-Very high blood sugar readings

Hyperparathyroidism.education:
What is Hyperparathyroidism?
Hyperparathyroidism is a condition in which one or more of the parathyroid glands produce too much parathyroid hormone (PTH). This causes calcium levels in the blood to rise too high (hypercalcemia), which can weaken bones, cause kidney stones, and affect the heart, muscles, and nervous system.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Fatigue or weakness
-Bone pain or fragile bones (osteoporosis)
-Kidney stones
-Frequent urination and excessive thirst
-Abdominal pain, nausea, or constipation
-Depression, confusion, or difficulty concentrating
-Muscle aches or cramps
-Joint pain
-Loss of appetite
-Some people may have no noticeable symptoms

Risk Factors:
-Being female
-Older age (especially postmenopausal women)
-Prolonged vitamin D deficiency
-History of radiation therapy to the head or neck
-Lithium use
-Genetic conditions such as Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN)
-Family history of hyperparathyroidism

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications as directed.
-Maintain adequate hydration unless restricted by the healthcare provider.
-Engage in regular weight-bearing exercise as tolerated to support bone health.
-Follow dietary recommendations regarding calcium and vitamin D intake.
-Monitor bone density as recommended.
-Complete laboratory testing for calcium, PTH, and kidney function as ordered.
-Report new or worsening bone pain, kidney stones, muscle weakness, or mood changes.
-Keep all scheduled endocrinology and PCP appointments.
-Discuss surgical options (parathyroidectomy) with the healthcare provider if recommended.

Hypothyroidism.education:
What is Hypothyroidism?
Hypothyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland does not produce enough thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormones regulate the body's metabolism, energy, and many vital functions. When thyroid hormone levels are too low, body processes slow down, leading to symptoms such as fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Fatigue or lack of energy
-Weight gain or difficulty losing weight
-Increased sensitivity to cold
-Constipation
-Dry skin and hair
-Hair loss or thinning
-Puffy face or swelling
-Hoarse voice
-Muscle weakness, aches, or stiffness
-Joint pain or stiffness
-Elevated cholesterol levels
-Slow heart rate
-Depression or mood changes
-Memory problems or difficulty concentrating
-Irregular or heavy menstrual periods

CKD.education:
What is Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)?
Chronic kidney disease is a condition in which the kidneys are damaged and cannot filter blood as well as they should. This can cause waste and excess fluid to build up in the body, leading to other health problems such as heart disease, anemia, and bone disease. CKD usually gets worse over time but can be managed to slow progression.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Fatigue or weakness
-Swelling of the feet, ankles, legs, or face
-Changes in urination (more or less frequent, foamy, dark, or blood-tinged)
-Nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite
-Persistent itching
-Muscle cramps, especially at night
-Shortness of breath
-Difficulty concentrating
-Trouble sleeping
-High blood pressure that is difficult to control
-Early CKD often has no symptoms

Risk Factors:
-Diabetes
-High blood pressure
-Heart disease
-Family history of kidney disease
-Obesity
-Older age
-Smoking
-Frequent use of NSAIDs or certain medications
-History of acute kidney injury
-African American, Hispanic, Native American, or Asian descent

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications as directed, including blood pressure and diabetes medications.
-Follow dietary restrictions for sodium, potassium, phosphorus, and protein as directed.
-Maintain blood pressure and blood sugar within the provider-recommended range.
-Stay physically active as tolerated.
-Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) unless approved by the healthcare provider.
-Do not take supplements or herbal remedies without consulting the provider.
-Complete all recommended laboratory tests and imaging.
-Keep all scheduled nephrology and PCP appointments.
-Discuss dialysis planning or transplant evaluation if CKD progresses.
-Stop smoking.

BPH.education:
What is Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)?
BPH is a non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland that commonly occurs in men as they age. The enlarged prostate can squeeze or partially block the urethra, causing urinary symptoms. BPH is not prostate cancer and does not increase the risk of cancer, but it can significantly affect quality of life if not managed.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Frequent urination, especially at night (nocturia)
-Difficulty starting urination
-Weak or interrupted urine stream
-Feeling that the bladder is not completely empty
-Urgency to urinate
-Dribbling at the end of urination
-Straining to urinate
-Urinary retention (inability to urinate)

Risk Factors:
-Older age (especially over 50)
-Family history of BPH
-Obesity
-Diabetes and heart disease
-Sedentary lifestyle
-Certain ethnic backgrounds

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed (alpha-blockers, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, or combination therapy).
-Report new or worsening urinary symptoms to the healthcare provider.
-Avoid medications that can worsen symptoms (decongestants, antihistamines) unless approved by the provider.
-Limit fluids in the evening to reduce nighttime urination.
-Avoid caffeine and alcohol, which can irritate the bladder.
-Urinate when the urge is first felt; do not delay.
-Practice double voiding (urinate, wait a moment, then try again).
-Stay physically active.
-Keep all scheduled urology and PCP appointments.

Urinary Incontinence.education:
What is Urinary Incontinence?
Urinary incontinence is the involuntary loss of urine. It is a common condition that can range from occasionally leaking urine when coughing or sneezing to having an urge to urinate that is so sudden and strong that it is difficult to reach a toilet in time. Urinary incontinence can affect quality of life but is treatable and manageable.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Leaking urine during physical activities (coughing, sneezing, laughing, exercising)
-Sudden, strong urge to urinate followed by involuntary loss of urine
-Frequent urination (more than 8 times in 24 hours)
-Nighttime urination
-Leaking urine without awareness
-Difficulty starting urination or weak urine stream
-Feeling that the bladder is not completely empty

Risk Factors:
-Older age
-Being female (pregnancy, childbirth, menopause)
-Prostate problems in men
-Obesity
-Neurological conditions
-Diabetes
-Chronic cough
-Pelvic surgery
-Urinary tract infections
-Certain medications

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Change incontinence products after each episode.
-Clean the skin gently after each episode.
-Pat the skin dry completely.
-Apply a barrier cream if recommended.
-Maintain adequate hydration unless restricted.
-Follow a regular toileting schedule.
-Wear clean, properly fitting absorbent products.
-Check the skin daily for redness, irritation, or breakdown.
-Wash hands before and after incontinence care.
-Practice pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) if recommended.
-Report fever, painful urination, blood in urine, worsening incontinence, or skin breakdown to the PCP promptly.
-Keep all scheduled urology, gynecology, and PCP appointments.

CVA/Stroke.education:
What is a Stroke (CVA)?
A stroke, or cerebrovascular accident, occurs when blood flow to a part of the brain is interrupted or reduced, depriving brain tissue of oxygen and nutrients. This can happen when a blood vessel is blocked by a clot (ischemic stroke) or when a blood vessel ruptures (hemorrhagic stroke). A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a temporary blockage that resolves but serves as a warning. Stroke is a medical emergency that requires immediate treatment.

Signs and Symptoms (BE FAST):
-B – Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination
-E – Eyes: Sudden vision changes in one or both eyes
-F – Face: Facial drooping or uneven smile
-A – Arms: Arm weakness or numbness
-S – Speech: Slurred speech or difficulty speaking or understanding
-T – Time: Call 911 immediately if any symptoms occur
-Sudden severe headache with no known cause
-Sudden confusion
-Sudden numbness or weakness, especially on one side

Risk Factors:
-High blood pressure (most significant risk factor)
-Atrial fibrillation
-Diabetes
-High cholesterol
-Smoking
-Obesity
-Physical inactivity
-Excessive alcohol use
-Heart disease
-Previous stroke or TIA
-Family history of stroke
-Older age
-Sickle cell disease

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications as directed, including blood thinners, blood pressure, cholesterol, and diabetes medications.
-Monitor blood pressure at home as directed.
-Participate in physical, occupational, and speech therapy as recommended.
-Follow a heart-healthy diet.
-Stay physically active as tolerated and approved by the provider.
-Stop smoking and avoid secondhand smoke.
-Limit alcohol intake.
-Know the BE FAST warning signs and teach them to family and caregivers.
-Attend all rehabilitation and follow-up appointments.
-Report new or recurring stroke symptoms immediately.

Multiple Sclerosis.education:
What is Multiple Sclerosis (MS)?
Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disease that affects the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord). The immune system attacks the protective covering (myelin) of nerve fibers, causing communication problems between the brain and the rest of the body. Over time, MS can cause permanent nerve damage or deterioration.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Numbness, tingling, or weakness in one or more limbs
-Electric-shock sensations with certain neck movements
-Tremor or lack of coordination
-Unsteady gait or difficulty walking
-Vision problems (blurred vision, double vision, partial or complete vision loss)
-Fatigue
-Dizziness or vertigo
-Slurred speech
-Bladder and bowel dysfunction
-Cognitive changes (difficulty with memory, attention, problem-solving)
-Muscle stiffness or spasms
-Pain

Risk Factors:
-Being female (2-3 times more common in women)
-Age 20 to 50
-Family history of MS
-Northern European descent
-Living farther from the equator
-Low vitamin D levels
-Smoking
-Certain autoimmune diseases
-Certain viral infections (Epstein-Barr virus)

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take disease-modifying therapies and other medications exactly as prescribed.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the neurologist.
-Participate in physical and occupational therapy as recommended.
-Stay physically active with appropriate exercise as tolerated.
-Manage fatigue through energy conservation strategies.
-Avoid overheating, which can temporarily worsen symptoms.
-Report new or worsening symptoms (relapses) to the neurologist promptly.
-Maintain a balanced diet and healthy weight.
-Manage stress through healthy coping strategies.
-Keep all scheduled neurology and PCP appointments.
-Complete recommended laboratory monitoring for disease-modifying therapies.

Parkinson Disease.education:
What is Parkinson's Disease?
Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurological disorder that affects movement and can also cause non-movement symptoms. It occurs when nerve cells in the brain that produce dopamine become damaged or die. Symptoms may gradually change over time. Treatment can help control symptoms and maintain independence and quality of life.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Tremors or shaking, commonly affecting the hands or arms
-Slowness of movement (bradykinesia)
-Muscle stiffness or rigidity
-Difficulty with balance or coordination
-Changes in walking, including small or shuffling steps
-Difficulty getting up from a chair or starting movement
-Changes in speech (softer, monotone) or facial expression
-Difficulty with handwriting or other fine motor activities
-Fatigue or sleep problems
-Constipation
-Depression, anxiety, or mood changes
-Memory or thinking changes
-Dizziness or lightheadedness, particularly when standing

Risk Factors:
-Older age (usually diagnosed after age 60)
-Male sex (slightly more common)
-Family history of Parkinson's disease
-Exposure to certain pesticides or herbicides
-Head trauma
-Certain genetic mutations

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take Parkinson's medications exactly as prescribed and at the scheduled times.
-Do not stop, skip, or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
-Use a pill organizer, written schedule, alarm, or phone reminder if needed.
-Keep an updated medication list and bring it to appointments.
-Report new or worsening symptoms or medication side effects to the neurologist.
-Notify the provider if medication appears to wear off sooner than expected.
-Remain physically active with walking, stretching, strengthening, and balance exercises.
-Participate in physical or occupational therapy when ordered.
-Change positions slowly, particularly when getting out of bed or standing.
-Use prescribed mobility or assistive devices consistently.
-Maintain regular appointments with the neurologist, PCP, and other specialists.

Seizure Disorders.education:
What are Seizure Disorders?
A seizure disorder, most commonly epilepsy, is a neurological condition characterized by recurrent, unprovoked seizures. Seizures occur when there is abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Seizures can vary from brief lapses of attention or muscle jerks to severe and prolonged convulsions.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Uncontrollable jerking movements of the arms and legs
-Temporary confusion or staring spells
-Loss of consciousness or awareness
-Fear, anxiety, or a sense of deja vu before a seizure (aura)
-Stiffening of the body
-Falling suddenly
-Lip smacking, chewing, or other repetitive movements
-Temporary loss of bladder or bowel control
-Difficulty speaking during or after a seizure
-Fatigue, confusion, or headache after a seizure

Risk Factors:
-Family history of seizures or epilepsy
-Head trauma or traumatic brain injury
-Stroke or other cerebrovascular disease
-Brain infections (meningitis, encephalitis)
-Brain tumors
-Developmental disorders
-Prenatal injury or birth complications
-Alzheimer's disease or other neurodegenerative conditions
-High fever in childhood (febrile seizures)

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take anti-seizure medications exactly as prescribed, at the same times each day.
-Do not stop, skip, or change medications without consulting the neurologist.
-Keep a seizure diary recording date, time, duration, and description of each seizure.
-Get adequate sleep on a regular schedule.
-Avoid known seizure triggers (sleep deprivation, excessive alcohol, flashing lights, stress).
-Wear medical identification indicating seizure disorder.
-Follow driving restrictions as required by state law and the healthcare provider.
-Inform family, friends, and coworkers about seizure first aid.
-Keep all scheduled neurology and PCP appointments.
-Complete recommended blood work to monitor anti-seizure medication levels.
-Discuss safety precautions for swimming, bathing, heights, and operating machinery.

Spinal Cord Injury.education:
What is a Spinal Cord Injury (SCI)?
A spinal cord injury is damage to the spinal cord that results in temporary or permanent changes in strength, sensation, and body functions below the site of injury. The severity depends on the location and extent of the damage. SCI can be complete (total loss of function below injury) or incomplete (some function remains).

Signs and Symptoms:
-Loss of movement or paralysis below the level of injury
-Loss of sensation (touch, heat, cold) below the level of injury
-Loss of bowel or bladder control
-Spasms or exaggerated reflexes
-Pain or stinging sensations
-Difficulty breathing or coughing
-Changes in sexual function and fertility
-Autonomic dysreflexia (dangerously high blood pressure in injuries above T6)

Risk Factors:
-Motor vehicle accidents
-Falls
-Violence (gunshot or stab wounds)
-Sports and recreation injuries
-Older age (increased fall risk)
-Osteoporosis
-Spinal canal narrowing

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Follow the rehabilitation plan and participate in physical and occupational therapy.
-Take all prescribed medications as directed.
-Perform regular skin checks to prevent pressure injuries.
-Follow bowel and bladder management programs as directed.
-Use prescribed mobility devices and adaptive equipment.
-Maintain respiratory hygiene if breathing is affected.
-Stay physically active as tolerated.
-Monitor for signs of autonomic dysreflexia (sudden severe headache, flushing, sweating above injury level).
-Prevent urinary tract infections through proper catheter care.
-Attend all rehabilitation, neurology, urology, and PCP appointments.
-Address mental health needs including depression and adjustment.

Traumatic Brain Injury.education:
What is Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI)?
A traumatic brain injury occurs when an external force causes damage to the brain. This can result from a blow, bump, or jolt to the head, or a penetrating head injury. TBI severity ranges from mild (concussion) to severe, and effects can be temporary or permanent.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Headache
-Confusion or disorientation
-Dizziness or loss of balance
-Nausea or vomiting
-Fatigue or drowsiness
-Difficulty speaking
-Memory problems or difficulty concentrating
-Mood changes, irritability, or depression
-Sleep disturbances
-Sensitivity to light or noise
-Blurred vision or ringing in the ears
-Seizures (in more severe cases)
-Loss of consciousness
-Weakness or numbness in extremities
-Persistent or worsening headache

Risk Factors:
-Falls (leading cause in older adults)
-Motor vehicle accidents
-Violence
-Sports and recreation injuries
-Military service and blast exposures
-Previous traumatic brain injury
-Older age or very young age
-Alcohol use

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Follow the healthcare provider's instructions for rest and activity progression.
-Take all prescribed medications as directed.
-Gradually return to normal activities as approved by the healthcare provider.
-Get adequate sleep and rest.
-Avoid activities that risk another head injury until cleared.
-Use memory aids such as calendars, lists, and reminders.
-Participate in rehabilitation therapies (physical, occupational, speech, cognitive).
-Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
-Wear protective equipment during sports and activities.
-Report new or worsening symptoms to the healthcare provider.
-Attend all follow-up neurology and PCP appointments.
-Address emotional and mental health needs.

Alzheimer's.education:
What is Alzheimer's Disease?
Alzheimer's disease is a progressive brain disorder that slowly destroys memory, thinking skills, and the ability to carry out daily activities. It is the most common cause of dementia in older adults. Alzheimer's worsens over time, but treatment and supportive care can help manage symptoms and maintain quality of life.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Memory loss that disrupts daily life
-Difficulty planning or solving problems
-Difficulty completing familiar tasks
-Confusion with time or place
-Trouble understanding visual images and spatial relationships
-New problems with words in speaking or writing
-Misplacing things and losing the ability to retrace steps
-Decreased or poor judgment
-Withdrawal from work or social activities
-Changes in mood and personality
-Wandering or getting lost

Risk Factors:
-Older age (greatest risk factor)
-Family history of Alzheimer's
-Genetics (APOE-e4 gene)
-Down syndrome
-Head trauma
-Cardiovascular disease risk factors
-Social isolation
-Low education levels

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed.
-Maintain a consistent daily routine.
-Use memory aids such as calendars, labeled photos, and written reminders.
-Keep the home safe by removing hazards and installing safety devices.
-Stay physically, mentally, and socially active as able.
-Ensure adequate nutrition and hydration.
-Attend all scheduled neurology, geriatrics, and PCP appointments.
-Plan for future care needs while the person can still participate in decisions.
-Seek caregiver support and respite care services.
-Address behavioral changes with the healthcare provider.

Anxiety.education:
What is an Anxiety Disorder?
Anxiety disorders involve more than temporary worry or fear. The anxiety does not go away and can get worse over time, interfering with daily activities, job performance, schoolwork, and relationships. Types include generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, and specific phobias.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Excessive worry or fear that is difficult to control
-Feeling restless, wound-up, or on edge
-Being easily fatigued
-Difficulty concentrating or mind going blank
-Irritability
-Muscle tension
-Sleep problems (difficulty falling or staying asleep, restless sleep)
-Panic attacks (sudden periods of intense fear with physical symptoms)
-Rapid heartbeat or pounding heart
-Shortness of breath
-Sweating, trembling, or shaking
-Avoidance of situations that trigger anxiety

Risk Factors:
-Family history of anxiety or other mental health disorders
-Childhood trauma or adverse experiences
-Chronic medical conditions
-Substance use or withdrawal
-Significant life stress
-Personality traits (shyness, behavioral inhibition)
-Being female
-History of other mental health disorders

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed (SSRIs, SNRIs, buspirone, or other medications).
-Attend therapy appointments (cognitive behavioral therapy is highly effective).
-Practice relaxation techniques such as deep breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or meditation.
-Stay physically active with regular exercise.
-Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
-Limit caffeine and alcohol.
-Stay connected with family, friends, or support groups.
-Identify and manage personal anxiety triggers.
-Avoid self-medicating with alcohol or drugs.
-Keep all scheduled behavioral health and PCP appointments.

Bipolar Disorder.education:
What is Bipolar Disorder?
Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition that causes extreme mood swings, including emotional highs (mania or hypomania) and lows (depression). These mood changes can affect sleep, energy, activity, judgment, behavior, and the ability to think clearly.

Signs and Symptoms:
Manic Episode:
-Abnormally upbeat, jumpy, or wired
-Increased activity, energy, or agitation
-Exaggerated sense of well-being and self-confidence
-Decreased need for sleep
-Unusual talkativeness or rapid speech
-Racing thoughts
-Distractibility
-Poor decision-making (spending sprees, risky behavior)

Depressive Episode:
-Depressed mood, sadness, or hopelessness
-Loss of interest or pleasure in activities
-Significant weight loss or gain
-Insomnia or sleeping too much
-Fatigue or loss of energy
-Feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt
-Difficulty thinking, concentrating, or making decisions
-Thoughts of death or suicide

Risk Factors:
-Family history of bipolar disorder
-Periods of high stress or trauma
-Drug or alcohol use
-Major life changes

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take mood-stabilizing and other psychiatric medications exactly as prescribed.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the psychiatrist, even when feeling well.
-Attend all therapy and psychiatric appointments.
-Maintain a regular daily routine including consistent sleep, meal, and activity times.
-Monitor mood changes and keep a mood diary.
-Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
-Identify early warning signs of manic and depressive episodes.
-Build a support network of family, friends, and support groups.
-Develop a crisis plan with the healthcare provider.
-Stay physically active.

Dementia.education:
What is Dementia?
Dementia is a general term for a decline in mental ability severe enough to interfere with daily life. It is not a specific disease but rather a group of symptoms associated with a decline in memory, reasoning, and other thinking skills. Alzheimer's disease is the most common type, but there are many other causes including vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, and frontotemporal dementia.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Memory loss, especially short-term memory
-Difficulty with communication and finding words
-Difficulty with complex tasks and problem-solving
-Difficulty with planning and organizing
-Confusion and disorientation
-Personality and behavior changes
-Depression and anxiety
-Inappropriate behavior
-Paranoia or suspiciousness
-Agitation
-Hallucinations (in some types)
-Difficulty with coordination and motor functions (in some types)
-Wandering

Risk Factors:
-Older age
-Family history of dementia
-Cardiovascular disease and risk factors
-Diabetes
-Smoking
-Excessive alcohol use
-Depression
-Social isolation
-Head trauma
-Down syndrome
-Low education and cognitive engagement

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed.
-Maintain a consistent daily routine.
-Keep the environment safe and familiar.
-Use memory aids and labels.
-Stay physically, mentally, and socially active as able.
-Ensure adequate nutrition and hydration.
-Manage behavioral symptoms with non-drug approaches first.
-Plan for future care needs while the person can participate.
-Attend all scheduled appointments.
-Seek caregiver support and respite care.
-Address legal and financial planning early.

Depression.education:
What is Depression?
Depression (major depressive disorder) is a common and serious mood disorder that causes persistent feelings of sadness and loss of interest. It affects how a person feels, thinks, and handles daily activities. Depression is not a weakness and requires treatment, which can be highly effective.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Persistent sad, anxious, or empty mood
-Feelings of hopelessness or pessimism
-Irritability
-Feelings of guilt, worthlessness, or helplessness
-Loss of interest or pleasure in hobbies and activities
-Decreased energy or fatigue
-Difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions
-Difficulty sleeping, early-morning awakening, or oversleeping
-Appetite and/or weight changes
-Thoughts of death or suicide
-Aches, pains, headaches, or digestive problems without a clear physical cause
-Restlessness

Risk Factors:
-Family history of depression
-Personal history of depression or other mental health disorders
-Major life changes, trauma, or stress
-Chronic medical conditions
-Certain medications
-Substance use
-Social isolation
-Being female

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take antidepressant medications as prescribed.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the healthcare provider.
-Attend therapy or counseling appointments.
-Stay physically active with regular exercise.
-Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
-Stay connected with family, friends, or support groups.
-Practice stress-reduction techniques.
-Set small, achievable goals.
-Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
-Report worsening symptoms or thoughts of suicide to the healthcare provider immediately.
-Keep all scheduled behavioral health and PCP appointments.

PTSD.education:
What is Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)?
PTSD is a mental health condition that can develop after experiencing or witnessing a traumatic event such as combat, natural disaster, serious accident, sexual assault, or other life-threatening event. Not everyone who experiences trauma develops PTSD, but those who do may have intense, disturbing thoughts and feelings related to the experience that persist long after the event.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Intrusive memories, flashbacks, or nightmares about the traumatic event
-Avoidance of people, places, activities, or situations that are reminders of the trauma
-Negative changes in thinking and mood (feeling hopeless, detached, emotionally numb)
-Loss of interest in activities previously enjoyed
-Feeling detached or estranged from others
-Difficulty experiencing positive emotions
-Being easily startled or frightened
-Hypervigilance (always being on guard)
-Trouble sleeping
-Difficulty concentrating
-Irritability, anger, or aggressive behavior
-Self-destructive behavior

Risk Factors:
-Exposure to traumatic events
-Prior trauma, especially childhood trauma
-Family or personal history of mental health disorders
-Lack of social support
-Ongoing stress after the event
-History of substance use
-Certain occupations (military, first responders, healthcare workers)

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed.
-Attend therapy appointments (trauma-focused CBT, EMDR, or prolonged exposure therapy).
-Practice coping skills learned in therapy.
-Stay connected with supportive family, friends, or support groups.
-Stay physically active.
-Maintain a regular sleep schedule.
-Avoid alcohol and drug use.
-Learn and practice grounding techniques.
-Identify triggers and develop a plan for managing them.
-Keep all scheduled behavioral health and PCP appointments.

Schizophrenia.education:
What is Schizophrenia?
Schizophrenia is a chronic and severe mental health disorder that affects how a person thinks, feels, and behaves. People with schizophrenia may seem like they have lost touch with reality. Symptoms usually start between ages 16 and 30 and fall into three categories: positive symptoms, negative symptoms, and cognitive symptoms.

Signs and Symptoms:
Positive symptoms:
-Hallucinations (hearing voices or seeing things that are not there)
-Delusions (false beliefs not based in reality)
-Thought disorders (unusual or dysfunctional ways of thinking)
-Movement disorders (agitated body movements)

Negative symptoms:
-Flat affect (reduced expression of emotions)
-Reduced feelings of pleasure in everyday life
-Difficulty beginning and sustaining activities
-Reduced speaking
-Social withdrawal

Cognitive symptoms:
-Poor executive functioning (difficulty understanding and using information)
-Difficulty focusing or paying attention
-Problems with working memory

Risk Factors:
-Family history of schizophrenia
-Brain chemistry and structure differences
-Prenatal exposure to viruses, malnutrition, or psychosocial factors
-Taking psychoactive drugs during adolescence
-Complications during birth

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take antipsychotic medications exactly as prescribed.
-Do not stop or change medications without consulting the psychiatrist, even when feeling better.
-Attend all therapy and psychiatric appointments.
-Participate in psychosocial treatments and rehabilitation.
-Maintain a consistent daily routine.
-Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs.
-Stay connected with supportive family, friends, or case managers.
-Report medication side effects to the healthcare provider.
-Develop a relapse prevention plan with the treatment team.
-Engage in meaningful activities and social connections as tolerated.

Substance-Related Disorders.education:
What are Substance-Related Disorders?
Substance-related disorders include substance use disorders (addiction) and substance-induced disorders. They involve the problematic use of alcohol, tobacco, illicit drugs, or prescription medications that leads to significant impairment or distress. Addiction is a chronic brain disorder, not a moral failing, and effective treatment is available.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Strong urges or cravings to use the substance
-Inability to limit or control use
-Needing more of the substance to get the same effect (tolerance)
-Withdrawal symptoms when not using the substance
-Continuing use despite negative consequences
-Neglecting responsibilities at home, work, or school
-Social withdrawal or giving up activities
-Using the substance in dangerous situations
-Spending significant time obtaining, using, or recovering from the substance
-Failed attempts to stop or cut down use
-Changes in behavior, mood, or appearance

Risk Factors:
-Family history of addiction
-Mental health disorders (depression, anxiety, PTSD, ADHD)
-Peer pressure and social environment
-Early use of substances
-Childhood trauma or adverse experiences
-Chronic pain and opioid use
-Easy access to substances
-Lack of social support

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Participate in treatment programs (inpatient, outpatient, medication-assisted treatment).
-Take prescribed medications as directed (naltrexone, buprenorphine, methadone, or others).
-Attend therapy or counseling sessions.
-Participate in support groups (AA, NA, SMART Recovery).
-Develop a relapse prevention plan.
-Identify and avoid personal triggers.
-Build a sober support network.
-Stay physically active.
-Maintain a regular daily routine.
-Address co-occurring mental health conditions.
-Keep all scheduled treatment and PCP appointments.

Cirrhosis.education:
What is Cirrhosis?
Cirrhosis is a late stage of scarring (fibrosis) of the liver caused by many forms of liver disease, including hepatitis and chronic alcoholism. The scar tissue replaces healthy liver tissue and prevents the liver from functioning normally. Cirrhosis cannot be reversed, but treatment can slow progression and manage complications.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Fatigue and weakness
-Easy bruising or bleeding
-Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)
-Itchy skin
-Swelling in the abdomen (ascites)
-Swelling of the legs and ankles
-Nausea and loss of appetite
-Weight loss
-Spider-like blood vessels on the skin
-Confusion, drowsiness, or slurred speech (hepatic encephalopathy)
-Dark urine
-Pale-colored stools

Risk Factors:
-Chronic alcohol use
-Chronic hepatitis B or C infection
-Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/NASH)
-Autoimmune hepatitis
-Bile duct diseases
-Certain genetic conditions
-Obesity and diabetes
-Certain medications or toxins

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take all prescribed medications as directed.
-Avoid all alcohol.
-Follow dietary restrictions for sodium and protein as directed.
-Take lactulose or rifaximin as prescribed for encephalopathy prevention.
-Weigh yourself daily and report sudden weight gain.
-Report new or worsening confusion, drowsiness, or personality changes.
-Complete recommended laboratory tests and imaging.
-Receive hepatitis A and B vaccinations if not already immune.
-Avoid NSAIDs and acetaminophen in excess.
-Discuss liver transplant evaluation with the provider if appropriate.
-Keep all scheduled hepatology and PCP appointments.

Crohn's Disease.education:
What is Crohn's Disease?
Crohn's disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that causes chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. It can affect any part of the GI tract from the mouth to the anus but most commonly affects the end of the small intestine and the beginning of the colon. Crohn's disease has periods of flare-ups and remissions.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Diarrhea (sometimes bloody)
-Abdominal pain and cramping
-Fatigue
-Unintended weight loss
-Fever
-Mouth sores
-Reduced appetite
-Perianal disease (pain, drainage, or fistulas near the anus)
-Joint pain
-Eye inflammation
-Skin rashes
-Delayed growth in children

Risk Factors:
-Family history of IBD
-Younger age (often diagnosed before age 30)
-Cigarette smoking (strongest controllable risk factor)
-Certain ethnic backgrounds (Ashkenazi Jewish descent)
-NSAIDs and certain medications may worsen the condition
-Living in urban or industrialized areas
-Diet high in processed foods

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed (aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, immunomodulators, biologics).
-Do not stop medications without consulting the gastroenterologist.
-Follow dietary recommendations from the healthcare team.
-Stay hydrated.
-Stop smoking.
-Manage stress.
-Keep a food diary to identify trigger foods.
-Complete recommended laboratory tests and colonoscopies.
-Report flare symptoms promptly.
-Keep all scheduled gastroenterology and PCP appointments.

Inflammatory Bowel Disease.education:
What is Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)?
Inflammatory bowel disease is a term for two conditions (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) that involve chronic inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. -Abdominal pain and cramping

-Urgency to have a bowel movement
-Fatigue
-Unintended weight loss
-Reduced appetite
-Fever during flares
-Joint pain
-Skin problems
-Eye inflammation

-Family history of IBD
-Age (most often diagnosed in teens and young adults)
-Certain ethnic backgrounds
-Cigarette smoking (increases risk for Crohn's)
-Environmental factors
-Prior use of NSAIDs or antibiotics

Treatment and Self-Management:

-Follow dietary recommendations.
-Stay hydrated, especially during flares.
-Stop smoking.
-Manage stress.

-Report flare symptoms promptly.

Liver Disease.education:
What is Liver Disease?
Liver disease refers to any condition that damages the liver and affects its function. The liver is essential for digesting food, storing energy, and removing toxins from the body. There are many types of liver disease, including hepatitis, fatty liver disease, and cirrhosis.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)
-Abdominal pain and swelling
-Swelling of the legs and ankles
-Itchy skin
-Dark urine
-Pale or bloody stools
-Chronic fatigue
-Nausea or vomiting
-Loss of appetite
-Easy bruising
-Confusion or difficulty thinking (in advanced disease)

Risk Factors:
-Heavy alcohol use
-Obesity
-Type 2 diabetes
-Hepatitis B or C infection
-Exposure to toxins or certain chemicals
-Certain medications
-Family history of liver disease
-Autoimmune conditions

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed.
-Avoid all alcohol.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Follow dietary recommendations.
-Avoid medications that can harm the liver (consult provider before taking any OTC medications).
-Get vaccinated for hepatitis A and B if not already immune.
-Complete recommended laboratory tests.
-Keep all scheduled hepatology and PCP appointments.
-Report new or worsening symptoms promptly.

NASH.education:
What is NASH (Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis)?
NASH is a form of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) in which there is inflammation and liver cell damage in addition to fat accumulation in the liver. NASH can progress to fibrosis (scarring), cirrhosis, and even liver failure. It is closely associated with obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Most people with NASH have no symptoms in early stages
-Fatigue
-Pain or discomfort in the upper right abdomen
-Enlarged liver
-Jaundice (in advanced cases)
-Swelling of the abdomen or legs (in advanced cases)
-Spider-like blood vessels (in advanced cases)
-General malaise

Risk Factors:
-Overweight or obesity
-Type 2 diabetes or insulin resistance
-High cholesterol or triglycerides
-Metabolic syndrome
-Polycystic ovary syndrome
-Sleep apnea
-Hypothyroidism
-Older age
-Hispanic or Asian ethnicity

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Lose weight gradually if overweight (7-10% body weight loss can improve NASH).
-Follow a healthy, balanced diet.
-Exercise regularly as tolerated.
-Control blood sugar, cholesterol, and triglycerides.
-Avoid alcohol.
-Avoid unnecessary medications that may stress the liver.
-Take prescribed medications as directed.
-Complete recommended laboratory tests and imaging.
-Keep all scheduled hepatology and PCP appointments.

Arthritis.education:
What is Arthritis?
Arthritis is a term for conditions that cause inflammation, pain, stiffness, and decreased movement of the joints. There are many types, including osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear) and rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune). Symptoms and treatment may vary depending on the type.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Joint pain
-Stiffness, especially in the morning or after inactivity
-Swelling of joints
-Redness and warmth around affected joints
-Decreased range of motion
-Fatigue
-Joint deformity (in advanced cases)
-Grinding or crunching sensation in the joints

Risk Factors:
-Older age
-Being female (rheumatoid arthritis)
-Family history of arthritis
-Previous joint injury
-Obesity (increases stress on weight-bearing joints)
-Smoking
-Certain occupations with repetitive joint stress

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take pain or arthritis medications as prescribed.
-Stay physically active with low-impact activities (walking, swimming, stretching).
-Protect joints and use proper body mechanics.
-Balance activity and rest.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Use heat or cold safely as recommended.
-Eat a balanced, anti-inflammatory diet.
-Prevent falls by keeping walking areas clear and wearing supportive footwear.
-Monitor symptoms and report persistent or worsening pain, swelling, or decreased mobility.
-Keep all scheduled PCP, rheumatology, or orthopedic appointments.

Back Pain.education:
What is Chronic Back Pain?
Chronic back pain is pain in the back that persists for 12 weeks or longer, even after an initial injury or underlying cause has been treated. It can range from a dull, constant ache to a sudden, sharp pain. Chronic back pain can significantly affect quality of life and daily activities.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Persistent aching or stiffness along the spine
-Sharp, localized pain in the neck, upper back, or lower back
-Pain that radiates from the low back to the buttock, leg, or foot (sciatica)
-Inability to stand straight without pain
-Muscle spasms
-Decreased range of motion
-Numbness or tingling in the legs or feet
-Pain that worsens with certain activities, prolonged sitting, or standing

Risk Factors:
-Older age
-Lack of physical activity
-Overweight or obesity
-Improper lifting techniques
-Smoking
-Psychological conditions (depression, anxiety, stress)
-Occupational factors (heavy lifting, prolonged sitting)
-Previous back injuries
-Degenerative disc disease or spinal conditions

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed.
-Stay physically active; avoid prolonged bed rest.
-Participate in physical therapy as recommended.
-Practice proper body mechanics and lifting techniques.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Use heat or cold therapy as recommended.
-Practice core-strengthening exercises.
-Maintain good posture.
-Use ergonomic furniture and support when sitting.
-Manage stress through relaxation techniques.
-Stop smoking.
-Keep all scheduled PCP, orthopedic, and physical therapy appointments.

DDD.education:
What is Degenerative Disc Disease (DDD)?
Degenerative disc disease is a condition in which the intervertebral discs (the cushions between the vertebrae of the spine) break down due to wear and tear over time. As discs degenerate, they lose height, flexibility, and their ability to cushion the spine, which can lead to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Pain in the neck, mid-back, or lower back
-Pain that may radiate to the arms, hands, buttocks, or legs
-Pain that worsens with sitting, bending, lifting, or twisting
-Pain that improves with walking, movement, or changing positions
-Numbness or tingling in the extremities
-Muscle weakness
-Stiffness in the spine
-Episodes of severe pain that gradually improve
-Decreased range of motion

Risk Factors:
-Aging (natural wear and tear)
-Repetitive physical activities
-Spinal injuries
-Obesity
-Smoking (reduces blood supply to discs)
-Genetics
-Occupations requiring heavy lifting or prolonged sitting

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed pain medications, anti-inflammatories, or muscle relaxants as directed.
-Participate in physical therapy to strengthen core and back muscles.
-Stay physically active with low-impact exercises.
-Maintain proper posture and body mechanics.
-Use heat or cold therapy as recommended.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Stop smoking.
-Use ergonomic supports when sitting or sleeping.
-Avoid activities that aggravate symptoms.
-Consider epidural steroid injections or surgical options if recommended.
-Keep all scheduled orthopedic, neurosurgery, and PCP appointments.

Osteoporosis.education:
What is Osteoporosis?
Osteoporosis is a condition in which bones become weak and brittle, increasing the risk of fractures. It occurs when the body loses too much bone, makes too little bone, or both. Osteoporosis-related fractures most commonly occur in the hip, spine, and wrist.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Osteoporosis is often called a "silent disease" because there are usually no symptoms until a fracture occurs
-Back pain caused by a fractured or collapsed vertebra
-Loss of height over time
-Stooped posture (kyphosis)
-A bone that breaks more easily than expected

Risk Factors:
-Being female (especially postmenopausal)
-Older age
-Small body frame
-Family history of osteoporosis or fractures
-Low calcium or vitamin D intake
-Sedentary lifestyle
-Smoking
-Excessive alcohol consumption
-Certain medications (long-term corticosteroids, some seizure medications)
-Certain medical conditions (rheumatoid arthritis, hyperthyroidism, celiac disease)
-Early menopause
-Low estrogen or testosterone levels

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed osteoporosis medications as directed (bisphosphonates, denosumab, or others).
-Take calcium and vitamin D supplements as recommended by the healthcare provider.
-Engage in regular weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercises.
-Prevent falls by removing home hazards, using handrails, wearing supportive shoes, and improving lighting.
-Avoid smoking.
-Limit alcohol intake.
-Complete bone density testing (DEXA scan) as recommended.
-Use proper body mechanics when lifting.
-Keep all scheduled PCP, endocrinology, or rheumatology appointments.

Anemia.education:
What is Anemia?
Anemia is a condition in which the blood does not have enough healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin to carry adequate oxygen to the body's tissues. There are many types of anemia with different causes, including iron deficiency, vitamin deficiency, chronic disease, and genetic conditions.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Fatigue and weakness
-Pale or yellowish skin
-Shortness of breath
-Dizziness or lightheadedness
-Cold hands and feet
-Rapid or irregular heartbeat
-Headache
-Chest pain
-Brittle nails
-Unusual cravings for non-food items (pica)
-Difficulty concentrating
-Leg cramps

Risk Factors:
-Diet lacking in iron, vitamin B12, folate, or vitamin C
-Chronic conditions (CKD, cancer, inflammatory diseases)
-Heavy menstrual periods
-Pregnancy
-GI conditions causing blood loss or malabsorption
-Family history (sickle cell, thalassemia)
-Older age
-Chronic infections
-Autoimmune disorders

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed iron, vitamin B12, folate, or other supplements as directed.
-Take iron supplements on an empty stomach with vitamin C to improve absorption (unless GI upset occurs).
-Avoid taking iron supplements with calcium, dairy, coffee, or tea.
-Eat iron-rich and nutrient-dense foods.
-Complete recommended laboratory tests to monitor hemoglobin and iron levels.
-Report worsening fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest pain.
-Address underlying causes with the healthcare provider.
-Keep all scheduled PCP and hematology appointments.

Sickle Cell Disease.education:
What is Sickle Cell Disease?
Sickle cell disease is a group of inherited red blood cell disorders in which hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen, is abnormal. This causes red blood cells to become rigid, sticky, and shaped like crescent moons (sickles). These sickle-shaped cells can block blood flow in small blood vessels, causing pain, organ damage, and other serious complications.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Episodes of severe pain (pain crises) in the chest, abdomen, joints, or bones
-Chronic pain
-Fatigue and anemia
-Swelling of the hands and feet (especially in young children)
-Frequent infections
-Delayed growth
-Vision problems
-Jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes)
-Shortness of breath
-Stroke symptoms
-Priapism (painful, prolonged erections)

Risk Factors:
-Inherited condition requiring sickle cell gene from both parents
-African American descent (most common in the US)
-Hispanic, Middle Eastern, South Asian, and Mediterranean descent

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Take prescribed medications as directed, including hydroxyurea and pain medications.
-Stay well-hydrated.
-Avoid extreme temperatures.
-Avoid high altitudes and unpressurized aircraft.
-Get regular exercise but avoid overexertion.
-Receive recommended vaccinations, including pneumococcal, meningococcal, influenza, and COVID-19.
-Take prescribed penicillin prophylaxis if directed.
-Complete regular health screenings (eyes, kidneys, lungs).
-Know the signs of stroke and splenic sequestration.
-Have a pain management plan for crises.
-Keep all scheduled hematology and PCP appointments.

Hearing Issues.education:
What are Hearing Issues?
Hearing loss is a partial or total inability to hear sounds in one or both ears. It can range from mild to profound and may be caused by aging, noise exposure, infections, genetics, or other medical conditions. Hearing loss can significantly affect communication, safety, and quality of life.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Difficulty hearing conversations, especially in noisy environments
-Frequently asking others to repeat themselves
-Turning up the volume on TV, radio, or phone
-Difficulty hearing on the telephone
-Muffled hearing
-Ringing, buzzing, or hissing in the ears (tinnitus)
-Difficulty understanding speech, especially high-pitched voices
-Withdrawal from social situations due to difficulty hearing
-Feeling that others are mumbling

Risk Factors:
-Aging (presbycusis)
-Chronic exposure to loud noises
-Family history of hearing loss
-Certain medications (ototoxic drugs)
-Chronic ear infections
-Head trauma
-Diabetes and cardiovascular disease
-Smoking

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Use prescribed hearing aids consistently and maintain them properly.
-Attend regular audiology appointments for hearing evaluations and hearing aid adjustments.
-Protect hearing by avoiding loud noise exposure and using ear protection.
-Face the speaker and maintain eye contact during conversations.
-Reduce background noise when possible.
-Use assistive listening devices, captioning, or visual alerts as needed.
-Keep ears clean but avoid inserting objects into the ear canal.
-Report sudden hearing loss, ear pain, or drainage immediately.
-Keep all scheduled audiology and ENT appointments.

References:

Cancer.education:
What is Cancer?
Cancer is a group of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells. If the spread is not controlled, it can result in death. Cancer can develop in almost any organ or tissue in the body. Treatment depends on the type, location, and stage of cancer.

Signs and Symptoms:
-Unexplained weight loss
-Fatigue that does not improve with rest
-Pain that does not go away
-Skin changes (darkening, yellowing, redness, sores that do not heal)
-Changes in bowel or bladder habits
-Persistent cough or trouble breathing
-Difficulty swallowing
-Unusual bleeding or discharge
-Lumps or thickening in the body
-Fever or night sweats
-Changes in moles or skin spots

Risk Factors:
-Older age
-Family history of cancer
-Tobacco use
-Excessive alcohol consumption
-Obesity
-Excessive sun exposure
-Exposure to radiation or certain chemicals
-Certain infections (HPV, hepatitis)
-Chronic inflammation
-Immunosuppression
-Sedentary lifestyle
-Poor diet

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Follow the treatment plan prescribed by the oncology team.
-Take all prescribed medications as directed.
-Attend all scheduled chemotherapy, radiation, or immunotherapy sessions.
-Report side effects from treatment to the oncology team.
-Maintain adequate nutrition and hydration.
-Stay physically active as tolerated.
-Manage pain with the healthcare provider's guidance.
-Attend follow-up appointments for monitoring and surveillance.
-Seek emotional and psychological support.
-Complete recommended cancer screenings for early detection.
-Address advance care planning.

Hx of Renal Cancer.education:
What is Renal Cancer (Kidney Cancer)?
Renal cancer, or kidney cancer, begins in the kidneys. The most common type in adults is renal cell carcinoma. For individuals with a history of renal cancer, ongoing surveillance and management of risk factors are important to monitor for recurrence and maintain overall kidney health.

Signs and Symptoms (of recurrence or ongoing issues):
-Blood in the urine (hematuria)
-Persistent pain in the side, back, or abdomen
-A lump or mass in the side or abdomen
-Unexplained weight loss
-Fatigue
-Fever not caused by infection
-Loss of appetite
-Bone pain (if metastatic)
-Swelling of the ankles or legs

Risk Factors:
-Smoking
-Obesity
-High blood pressure
-Family history of kidney cancer
-Certain genetic conditions (Von Hippel-Lindau disease)
-Long-term dialysis
-Exposure to certain chemicals
-Older age
-Male sex

Treatment and Self-Management:
-Follow the surveillance schedule recommended by the oncologist (imaging, labs).
-Take prescribed medications as directed.
-Monitor remaining kidney function with regular lab work.
-Maintain blood pressure within the recommended range.
-Maintain a healthy weight.
-Stop smoking.
-Stay physically active as tolerated.
-Report new or recurring symptoms immediately.
-Keep all scheduled oncology, urology, nephrology, and PCP appointments.
